Separately, HB 2756 (data center cost-shifting protection) passed the House 38-19 and cleared a Senate committee but died when the Legislature adjourned sine die on June 13, 2026 without a final floor vote. On July 1, 2026 Hobbs vetoed HB 2873, which would have allowed referendum petitions to be withdrawn before a vote — a bill written in response to the Marana 'Project Blue' data center referendum fight. Hobbs also vetoed several AI bills on June 19, 2026, including chatbot-safety HB 2311 and synthetic intimate imagery HB 2133. Tucson's Project Blue data center faced local opposition. On August 13, 2026 Tucson approved its first large-scale data center regulations in a 6-1 vote: facilities over 25,000 square feet or 20 MW must maintain a half-mile residential buffer, cap building height at 50 feet, disclose energy sources, stay within potable water limits, and obtain mayor and council approval.

states.name: Arkansas
states.summary: Arkansas has no statewide moratorium or restriction legislation and still courts large projects, but county-level restriction spread rapidly in August 2026 and several of the pauses are among the longest in the country. Independence County's quorum court unanimously enacted a five-year moratorium on August 10, 2026 — running through 2031 — citing strain on local water supply despite having no specific project proposed. Madison County followed on August 17 with a unanimous 8-0 three-year moratorium, also with no known project in development; it is the second-longest pause in the state and one of five Arkansas counties with three-year or longer moratoriums. Union County and Carroll County each adopted one-year pauses in June 2026, and Russellville adopted a six-month moratorium in July. Central Arkansas has taken the regulatory route instead. The Pulaski County Quorum Court voted down a 12-month construction moratorium 10-3 on July 28, 2026 amid disputes over an exemption for the AVAIO Digital Wrightsville project, and a Little Rock moratorium proposal failed on a 4-4 deadlock on August 4. Both jurisdictions are instead writing rules: Little Rock passed regulations in June 2026, and on August 13 Pulaski County advanced an ordinance classifying large facilities as heavy industrial, requiring a conditional use permit, 500-foot residential setbacks and noise caps, but the ordinance drew an overflow crowd at the August 25 meeting and the final vote was delayed. Separately, a county judge dismissed a newspaper public-records suit seeking Google's utility rate contract for its $4 billion West Memphis data center, ruling the dispute belongs before the state Public Service Commission.

states.name: California
states.summary: No statewide moratorium legislation; several bills (AB 2469, AB 2383, AB 1577, SB 1168, SB 887) are in committee, with the Legislature in summer recess until August 3, 2026. Local action is accelerating: Imperial County extended its data center pause to a full year on July 14, 2026, and Monterey Park's moratorium runs through January 2027. Indio's council unanimously extended its own moratorium on July 15, 2026. Some jurisdictions have also imposed water-use restrictions affecting proposed sites. Community pressure is also killing projects outright: developer Eight Form withdrew its El Segundo data center application on July 9, 2026 at the close of a three-hour Planning Commission hearing focused on electricity demand. August brought California's first county-level pause of the wave: Tulare County's Board of Supervisors approved a 45-day moratorium on August 19, 2026 covering unincorporated areas while it evaluates public health and infrastructure impacts, with activists immediately pressing for a permanent ban. Coachella's City Council took up an ordinance banning data centers citywide on August 13, which would make it the third Riverside County city to do so after Perris and Desert Hot Springs. Hanford issued a policy statement on August 15 opposing data centers absent meaningful local review, noting its zoning already prohibits them. In Gilroy, Amazon began building on 56 acres of farmland under a 45-year-old zoning rule, with residents saying they were unaware until construction started because the comment period closed in 2024. The Coachella Valley hardened further in late August: Coachella's council passed its permanent citywide ban on August 25, and Palm Springs approved a 45-day moratorium on large-scale data centers on August 26 to study water, energy and infrastructure impacts before adopting permanent rules. The Legislature closed its 2026 session in early September by passing a slate of data center bills now on the Governor's desk: SB 1168 (McNerney), approved 38-0 in the Senate after a unanimous Assembly vote, directs the CPUC to ensure data centers pay their fair share of transmission and distribution costs; SB 886 (Padilla) requires a separate electricity rate class for data centers; and SB 887 requires environmental impact review. Local action continued: Mendocino County adopted a 45-day urgency ban on September 1, Escondido passed a 45-day AI data center moratorium in late August, and Fresno's council voted 7-0 on September 3 to begin drafting a 10-year citywide ban backed by Mayor Jerry Dyer. In Imperial County, a tentative court ruling sided with the City of Imperial's challenge to a data center approval, citing substantial evidence of adverse energy, water, air quality, noise and traffic impacts.

states.name: Florida
states.summary: Governor Ron DeSantis signed SB 484 — the Florida Hyperscale Data Center Act — into law on May 7, 2026 (effective July 1). The law classifies data centers consuming 50+ MW at peak demand as 'large-scale,' bars utilities from passing data center costs onto residential and small-business ratepayers, requires data centers to pay their full cost of service, creates a permitting framework to protect aquifers and local water (mandating reclaimed water where feasible), and preserves local government authority to deny or impose stricter standards on data center projects. Florida continues to attract data center investment, particularly in the Miami and Jacksonville markets, but local pushback emerged in mid-2026: Sarasota County adopted a one-year hyperscale moratorium in July, DeSoto County moved toward one, and Lakeland approved a one-year moratorium on first reading July 21, 2026 (final reading August 3). Governor DeSantis was one of only three governors — along with New Hampshire's Ayotte and Vermont's Scott — who declined to sign the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge expanded on July 23, 2026. Local restriction widened in August 2026. Washington County's commissioners unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on August 20 halting acceptance, processing, review and approval of data center applications in unincorporated areas, exempting only facilities where computer equipment occupies no more than 5% of gross floor area with demand under 250 kW. In Palm Beach County, commissioners voted 5-1 in July to reject Project Tango — a $2 billion AI campus — without prejudice after water-demand estimates diverged sharply between the developer's 5,000-gallon daily figure and county staff's 100,000-gallon projection, and approved a temporary halt on large-scale applications that went to a public hearing on August 27. Late August brought the first regulatory test of SB 484: the Public Service Commission is reviewing Duke Energy's first large-load proposal under the law, weighing whether it adequately shields ratepayers from data center costs, with a written order expected after post-hearing briefs. Martin County commissioners voted 4-1 on August 27 to put a moratorium discussion on their next agenda, while Tallahassee commissioners rejected a proposed AI data center ban 3-2 the same day, noting existing zoning already excludes such facilities. In early September 2026 Indiantown's Village Council rejected a proposed hyperscale application pause 4-1 — firing the village manager and removing the village attorney the same night — while North Port scheduled a moratorium vote for September 8.

states.name: Georgia
states.summary: All statewide data center bills (HB 1012 moratorium, SB 408 and SB 410 tax exemption repeal) failed when the 2026 legislative session ended. Local momentum continues: Camden County's Board of Commissioners voted on May 5, 2026 to adopt a six-month moratorium (the first on Georgia's coast) amid a contested industrial-park rezoning push, and Lee County commissioners weighed extending their existing moratorium in late May. Local action continued through July 2026: Walker County adopted a 30-day application moratorium on July 10 with a 180-day extension pending an August 6 hearing, Marietta adopted a temporary moratorium through December 31, and DeKalb County extended its pause into early 2027. Multiple counties in central/west Georgia retain active moratoriums including DeKalb, Pike, Lamar, Troup counties and the City of LaGrange. Atlanta requires special use permits within the Beltline radius. Cherokee County joined on July 22, 2026 with a 30-day moratorium that commissioners plan to extend into early 2027, and residents in Dalton — which third-party data shows has the highest documented data center count in its region — are organizing for a pause over the county administrator's objection. Governor Brian Kemp was among the 23 Republican governors who signed the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge on July 23, 2026. Albany adopted a 12-month moratorium in early August 2026. On August 13 the Marietta City Council voted 5-2 to approve an 11-acre data center despite the city's own six-month moratorium, because developer Prime Group Holdings' application predated the pause; dozens of residents protested. Montgomery County gave first reading to a strict ordinance requiring a 1,500-foot buffer, a three-mile separation from water bodies and farmland, and a no-tax-abatement pledge. Development also continues at scale: on August 3 Effingham County approved OpenAI's Project Camellia, a $20 billion, 1,440-acre campus with a 50% property tax abatement for 15 years and $32 million for local schools. A Maysville City Council meeting was adjourned after 14 minutes on August 3 when an update on the Northern Data/Rumble project drew shouting from the audience. Early September 2026 brought further local action: Forest Park approved a 90-day moratorium to draft zoning rules, Dougherty County unanimously extended its moratorium another 180 days on August 31, and Bulloch County commissioners rejected a permanent ban 4-3 while keeping their existing moratorium through the end of 2026.

On May 4-14, 2026 the Indianapolis City-County Council unanimously passed a non-binding resolution (Proposal 158) urging the Metropolitan Development Commission to pause data center approvals until May 7, 2027 or until tighter rules are adopted; the MDC is expected to discuss draft special development standards at its June 3, 2026 meeting. In mid-July 2026 an Indianapolis City-County Council committee approved a binding moratorium on new data center approvals through December 31, 2027, and Valparaiso's council advanced its own moratorium ordinance. The Indianapolis pause became binding on August 10, 2026, when the City-County Council voted 23-1 to bar new data center construction in Marion County through the end of 2027, giving councilors time to finalize noise, water management and electrical capacity rules; the Metropolitan Development Commission ratified it on August 19. Three previously approved projects — DC Blox in Warren Township, Metrobloks in Martindale-Brightwood, and Sabey in Decatur Township — are unaffected. Elkhart County held a first reading on August 18 of a moratorium covering data centers and battery storage running to December 31, 2027, with a special meeting for public comment and a vote on August 27. In St. Joseph County, a vote on expanding the AM General TIF district to include a Microsoft data center — which would let the county borrow up to $4 million — was postponed to September 22 amid questions about tax revenue distribution. Nearly a third of Indiana counties have now moved to restrict data centers. The City of Elkhart's council voted 9-0 on August 27, 2026 to stop accepting data center and battery storage applications until December 2027 while it studies grid, water, safety, traffic and noise impacts — a pause that covers only the city, with the separate county-level moratorium still pending. Applies only to the city, not Elkhart County.

states.name: Iowa
states.summary: No statewide moratorium, but Iowa has significant local action. Clarke and Johnson counties enacted moratoriums, Linn County passed one of the nation's strictest data center zoning ordinances with 1,000-foot setbacks and water study requirements, and Dubuque County supervisors approved a 12-month moratorium on May 26, 2026. Johnson County is now advancing what would be among the region's strictest data center ordinances — including closed-loop cooling requirements and designated development areas — despite having no active project applications; officials describe the intent as discouraging rather than banning facilities. On August 19, 2026 Maquoketa ended preliminary discussions with developer Gronen over a facility at the South Highway 61 Industrial Park, clarifying that no nondisclosure agreements had been signed, and said it will review its Heavy Industrial District regulations governing future data center development. Salix's council rejected a one-year moratorium 3-2 on August 21 after Google was revealed as the developer behind a local project, and Cedar Rapids announced housing incentives on August 27 to absorb the influx of data center construction workers.

One-year moratorium on rezoning, site plans, and building permits for data centers in unincorporated areas. Concerns about water pollution, power usage, and facility siting.

One of the nation's strictest local data center zoning ordinances. Requires comprehensive water studies, 1,000-foot residential setbacks, noise and light limits, and community betterment fund contributions.
Indefinite moratorium. Triggered by 200 MW Applied Digital proposal.
Commissioners approved moratorium while creating an ordinance

In its third consecutive meeting on the subject, the City Council voted 5-2 on July 28, 2026 to schedule an August 10 public hearing on a four-month data center moratorium; Councilors Jeff Schneider and Greg Nichols opposed. The city administrator said she would recommend suspending the additional-reading requirement so the council could take final action on the ordinance at that same August 10 meeting. states.name: Kansas
states.summary: No statewide data center legislation, but Kansas local action accelerated sharply in July 2026. Lawrence city commissioners unanimously adopted a two-year moratorium on large-scale data centers on July 14, 2026 — doubling an originally proposed one-year pause — while staff study long-term code changes. Lyon County commissioners approved a six-month moratorium on July 23, 2026 covering data centers and battery energy storage (through January 22, 2027), alongside a separate solar moratorium expiring December 1, 2026. Emporia took the opposite tack on July 22, 2026, approving three ordinances creating a digital infrastructure district with zoning protections; a citizen petition to prohibit data centers outright was not acted on and could reach the November 2026 ballot. Sedgwick County and Harvey County retain earlier moratoriums and Miami County has considered a one-to-two-year pause.

localMoratoriums.description: 90-day moratorium on data center permits, extended to June 11, 2026. Two data center developers seeking 1,000+ acres in western Sedgwick County.
County Commission considering a moratorium lasting one to two years while developing regulations. Prompted by Osawatomie's $1B data center proposal.
~3 year moratorium on data centers in unincorporated areas.
City Commission unanimously approved a two-year moratorium on large-scale data centers, extending an originally proposed one-year pause, while staff study longer-term code changes.

County Commission approved a six-month moratorium on data centers and battery energy storage systems, in effect until January 22, 2027, plus a separate commercial solar moratorium expiring December 1, 2026.

City Commission approved three ordinances establishing a digital infrastructure district and associated zoning protections. A citizen petition seeking an outright data center prohibition was not acted upon and could advance to the November 2026 ballot.

states.name: Kentucky
states.summary: Kentucky has no statewide data center moratorium and continues to court large projects, but its largest city has now paused new development. Louisville Metro Council voted 24-1 on August 13, 2026 to adopt a six-month moratorium blocking planners from approving new data center proposals until the council adopts comprehensive zoning rules, after the Planning and Zoning Committee advanced it 7-1 on August 4. Protesters at the vote pressed for a full year. The pause is meant to give the council time to study energy and water demand, infrastructure needs, tax implications and neighborhood noise; on August 20 the Louisville Planning Commission moved to strengthen the underlying restrictions. Nicholasville passed its own six-month moratorium on August 11, with residents citing electric bills, property taxes and water. Local restriction now spans a dozen Kentucky jurisdictions. Separately, a planned Paducah campus has been caught up in a proposed federal ban on AI data centers on certain federal land. The wave continued into September 2026: Rowan County's Fiscal Court approved a two-year moratorium on large-scale data centers (the county lacks zoning and will study a conditional-use process), and Winchester's commissioners unanimously passed a one-year moratorium within city limits.

Fiscal Court approved a six-month moratorium on data center applications as a proactive measure, despite no expressed developer interest.
Fiscal Court adopted countywide moratorium on new data center and large-scale IT infrastructure facility applications. Also rejected a rezoning proposal for a 138-acre data center site.

Magistrates cited two pending data center proposals, including at least one hyperscale facility, and the City of Burgin's effort to annex land for a data center; Burgin would need its own separate ordinance.

A standing-room-only public forum on July 29, 2026 drew near-unanimous resident opposition, with essentially every hand in the room raised against future data centers. Judge-Executive Jason Marshall said he would ask the fiscal court for a long-term moratorium to allow the county time to study infrastructure, farmland, utility and emergency-service impacts; the vote was scheduled for August 11, 2026. There are no current data center proposals or agreements in the county.

City passed a six-month moratorium on data centers as residents sought time to understand impacts on electric bills, property taxes and water.

Fiscal Court approved a two-year moratorium on large-scale data centers in early September 2026; the county has no zoning regulations and plans to consider a conditional-use review process during the pause. No projects have been proposed.

The Board of Commissioners unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on data center development within city limits in early September 2026, citing a lack of specific zoning rules and unresolved questions about utilities, rates and the environment; the rest of Clark County is not covered.

states.name: Louisiana
states.summary: No statewide moratorium legislation, but New Orleans enacted a one-year citywide ban on data center construction in January 2026. Louisiana continues to attract major data center investment in northern parishes. Governor Jeff Landry joined President Trump at the July 23, 2026 White House roundtable expanding the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, which commits signatories to keeping data center infrastructure and generation costs off other utility customers. On August 13, 2026 the Louisiana Public Service Commission voted 3-1 to let Meta keep details of its Richland Parish data center confidential, overruling an administrative law judge's subpoena for job and energy-use data; a trial on Entergy's $13 billion power plant expansion is set for October with a decision expected in December. On August 18 a Caddo Parish commissioner proposed a two-year moratorium on tax incentives for data centers, referred to the special projects committee — though the parish attorney noted state law requires a master plan before a moratorium can be adopted.

localMoratoriums.description: City Council voted 6-0 to impose a one-year ban on data center construction, expansion, or establishment citywide. Could last up to 2 years.

A commissioner proposed a two-year moratorium on tax incentives for data centers; referred to the special projects committee. The parish attorney noted state law requires a master plan before a moratorium can be adopted.

states.name: Maine
states.summary: On April 29, 2026, Maine's Legislature failed to override Governor Mills' veto of LD 307 — the House voted 72-65 and the Senate 20-11, both falling short of the two-thirds majority required. The decisive defeat ends the path for what would have been the first statewide data center moratorium in US history. Mills had vetoed LD 307 on April 24 because it lacked an exemption for the planned Jay data center at the former Androscoggin Mill site. She separately signed LD 713 (banning data centers from Maine's business development tax incentive programs) and on April 29, 2026 issued Executive Order 5 establishing the 15-member Maine Data Center Advisory Council, which is due to deliver recommendations by January 29, 2027. Local moratoria remain active in Bangor and other communities; Scarborough and Brunswick each enacted 180-day moratoria in early June 2026, and Warren voters approved one on July 8. The veto override defeat has prompted national reflection in moratorium-curious states. On August 27, 2026 Eastport's Planning Board unanimously recommended a permanent ban on data centers across all of the city's zoning districts, sending the question to the city council.

states.name: Maryland
states.summary: Maryland HB 120 (data center construction moratorium unless co-located with generation) died in committee when the General Assembly adjourned in early April 2026, but county governments have made Maryland one of the most restricted states in the country. Howard County unanimously passed CB31-2026 — the S.M.A.R.T. Siting Act — on June 1, 2026, halting new data center development through November 2, 2027 and creating a study task force. Prince George's County enacted a two-year pause on hyperscale development on July 7, 2026 (liftable early if a zoning framework is adopted). On May 11, 2026 the Baltimore City Council passed Bill 26-0158, a one-year moratorium on data centers using 10 MW or more plus a nine-month impact study. On July 22, 2026 Montgomery County Council committees voted unanimously to merge two competing bills into a single 18-month moratorium and send it to the full council, building on County Executive Elrich's six-month executive-order pause from June. Baltimore County and Frederick County restrictions also remain in place. Prince George's County extended its hyperscale pause in early August 2026. On August 9, Amazon withdrew a planned campus near the Calvert Cliffs Nuclear Power Plant, citing internal infrastructure planning rather than local opposition; Calvert County is pursuing a six-month moratorium regardless.

Local pauses continue to accumulate: Westfield's City Council gave final unanimous approval to a 12-month moratorium on July 6, 2026, joining earlier action in Lowell, Everett, and Shutesbury.

states.name: Michigan
states.summary: Michigan introduced a bipartisan House bill package (HB 5594-5596) proposing a one-year moratorium preventing EGLE and local governments from issuing data center permits until April 2027. Governor Whitmer has explicitly stated she would veto any moratorium legislation, calling it 'an automatic non-starter.' More than 20 Michigan townships and cities have enacted local moratoria independently — the most of any state — with Meridian Township, Macomb County's Washington Township, and the City of Flint (a one-year pause on June 8, 2026) among the most recent. In June 2026 legislators renewed the statewide push: HB 5594-5596 (House) and companion SB 1018-1020 (Senate) were introduced to halt data center development until April 1, 2027, and Senate Democrats unveiled a separate eight-bill regulatory package — though none has been enacted. On July 15, 2026 Governor Whitmer unveiled the Michigan Affordable and Responsible Growth Action Plan, pairing a call for lawmakers to codify consumer and energy-cost guardrails in statute with a voluntary industry pledge — residents never pay for data center energy demand, companies build or buy additional energy resources, grid reliability and freshwater protection commitments, and jobs and community benefits. Google and Oracle announced support the same day. Whitmer continues to oppose a statewide moratorium. Kalamazoo's City Commission approved a resolution on August 18, 2026 enacting a one-year data center moratorium, with the community divided over whether the temporary pause should become a permanent ban. Bay City's planning commission formed a subcommittee on August 20 to study a draft ordinance addressing facility size, power demand, water use, noise and decommissioning, with a revisit scheduled for October. Garfield Charter Township (Grand Traverse County) unanimously adopted a one-year moratorium on data centers and crypto mining on August 25, 2026, extendable to 18 months, to study water and power impacts. Wixom ended its six-month moratorium early in September 2026 and replaced it with stricter zoning — a 1,500-foot setback from homes, schools and parks, a well-water ban and mandatory sound studies — as developer Wixom Industrial One LLC pressed a federal lawsuit over the pause.

states.name: Minnesota
states.summary: Minnesota enacted SF 608 (June 2025) restricting enterprise data centers to industrial districts statewide. The 2026 statewide moratorium bills (HF 4888 and SF 4298) died when the Legislature adjourned sine die on May 18, 2026 without either receiving a committee hearing. Local action accelerated: on May 21, 2026 the Minneapolis City Council voted 8-5 to enact a six-month interim moratorium on data centers larger than 350,000 sq ft (the downtown core is exempt), giving final approval on June 25. Inver Grove Heights approved its own one-year moratorium on June 26, 2026 despite a developer's litigation threat, while Eagan — the first Minnesota city to enact a data center moratorium — was sued on June 15 by a developer seeking to void its pause. North Mankato is refining a moratorium targeting facilities over 150,000 square feet or using 50,000 or more gallons of water daily, with a second public hearing and council vote pending as of August 18, 2026.

states.name: Mississippi

Local resistance emerged in July 2026: on July 14, 2026 the Jackson City Council voted 5-2 for a 183-day moratorium on data centers — the first in the state — with members saying the capital is 'not ready for a data center.' In Warren County, residents have rallied against a proposed Amazon data center near Vicksburg, citing noise, pollution, utility costs, and its proximity to an elementary school.

states.name: Missouri
states.summary: No statewide moratorium legislation, but Missouri is a hotbed of local action. St. Charles enacted a citywide moratorium and is considering a permanent ban. Kansas City and St. Louis enacted zoning restrictions, and Columbia froze permits. Jackson County passed a 180-day moratorium (8-0) on June 22, 2026, and Springfield followed with a 120-day administrative delay on June 29. In mid-July 2026 the pace picked up again: St. Charles County unanimously approved a six-month moratorium on July 13 and the City of St. Joseph paused new applications the same day. Missouri also landed two of the nation's largest 2026 data center announcements — a $15B Google campus and a $10B Amazon campus, both in Montgomery County. Kansas City is now reviewing a 20-story downtown data center that would redevelop the historic Western Newspaper Union building; more than 80 residents turned out against it over water demand and preservation concerns, and the City Planning Commission takes it up August 5, 2026. On August 12, 2026 state lawmakers announced plans for AI and data center legislation when the General Assembly reconvenes in January 2027, and released an evaluation framework for local governments assessing proposals. Local decisions continue to cut both ways: St. Joseph's council rejected a proposal to create a citizen data center advisory committee 3-6 on August 17, with opponents arguing existing committees already provide oversight. Ozark's Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously recommended preemptive data center regulations on August 25, 2026 — requiring a conditional use permit, environmental impact report, noise compliance and size/use disclosure — which now go to the Board of Aldermen.

states.name: Montana
states.summary: No statewide moratorium despite significant lobbying efforts, but county-level action has begun. On July 9, 2026 Missoula County commissioners approved an interim zoning moratorium of up to one year on new data centers while permanent regulations are drafted; the county separately requires data center and crypto operations to offset 100% of electrical consumption with new renewable energy. Up to 14 data centers have been proposed statewide. In Butte-Silver Bow, a district court judge is weighing a lawsuit over rejected signatures on a data center ballot initiative: the county clerk accepted 3,652 signatures on July 31, 2026 but rejected the initiative on August 10, and as of August 20 the judge had sought additional briefing with a decision expected within a week.

states.name: Nebraska
states.summary: Nebraska has significant data center activity with Google facilities in Papillion, Omaha, and Lincoln, plus new mega-proposals. Gage County's Planning & Zoning Commission unanimously recommended an 18-month moratorium on June 16, 2026, now awaiting a Board of Supervisors vote; several other Nebraska counties already have moratoriums. Broken Bow adopted a six-month moratorium on July 15, 2026, extendable by up to 12 more months. Governor Jim Pillen joined President Trump at the July 23, 2026 White House roundtable expanding the Ratepayer Protection Pledge. County-level rulemaking advanced in August 2026. Lincoln County set a timeline for finalizing data center regulations, holding a public hearing August 11 in North Platte and targeting August 31 for a final hearing on a zoning ordinance requiring closed-loop cooling, proof that infrastructure costs will not shift to ratepayers, and residential screening. Broken Bow gave first reading to an ordinance requiring noise studies, decommissioning bonds at 150% of costs, and foreign ownership disclosure. Gage County commissioners held a public hearing in early September 2026 — drawing about 30 speakers citing water, land use and property-value concerns — on extending the county's data center pause from 8 to 18 months, with a decision expected within two weeks.

states.name: Nevada
states.summary: Nevada, particularly the Reno-Sparks area, is a major data center market with state tax abatements for qualifying facilities. On May 14, 2026 the Reno City Council voted 6-1 for a temporary moratorium on new data center construction permits (through December 31, 2026 or until new rules are adopted) — the first Nevada local government to do so — with four pipeline projects exempted. On June 1, 2026 the Council voted 6-1 to extend the moratorium through August 31, 2027 (or until new regulations are adopted). Not all Nevada cities followed: on July 22, 2026 the Henderson City Council rejected a proposed 180-day moratorium in favor of case-by-case development agreements. Separately, Boulder City is seeking a construction stay and Interior Board of Land Appeals relief after learning the BLM authorized a data center by amending an existing 2023 solar permit rather than opening a new public review. Nevada's first countywide ban followed on August 19, 2026, when Nye County commissioners voted 5-0 to prohibit data centers in the Pahrump Valley and the Basin 162 groundwater area after a meeting that drew hundreds of attendees and more than two hours of public comment. A companion measure (No. 2026-14) establishes land-use regulations and special use permitting for data centers elsewhere in the county.

Governor Ayotte was one of only three governors — with Florida's DeSantis and Vermont's Scott — who declined to sign the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge when it was expanded on July 23, 2026. states.name: New Jersey
states.summary: New Jersey enacted its first data center ratepayer-protection law: A796/S731 (the 'Data Center Fair Share'/large-load tariff act) passed both chambers on June 30, 2026 and Governor Mikie Sherrill signed it into law on July 7, 2026 as part of a package of energy-affordability bills projected to save ratepayers over $1 billion per year. It directs the Board of Public Utilities to create a dedicated rate class and tariff for large data centers (50+ MW), requiring them to commit to paying at least 85% of projected power costs for 10 years and to post financial security so costs are not shifted to other ratepayers; the BPU has 12 months to set standards. The law follows Sherrill's May 27, 2026 comprehensive data center plan (ratepayer protection, power/water reporting, community benefit agreements). Companion bill S3379 (semi-annual water and energy reporting) remains in committee, and about 60 organizations continue to push for a stronger three-year moratorium on facilities over 20 MW. Pemberton Township became the first NJ municipality to ban data centers outright; Phillipsburg passed a final ban ordinance on April 14. On August 13, 2026 the Bayonne City Council unanimously prohibited data centers citywide and Mayor Sharon Ashe-Nadrowski signed the ordinance, making Bayonne the third New Jersey municipality with an outright ban after Pemberton Township and Phillipsburg. Municipal bans accelerated sharply in late August 2026: Stafford Township (Ordinance 2026-22) became Ocean County's first outright ban, Jackson Township followed with a 4-1 vote on August 25 (Ordinance 2026-25) citing grid, water and Pinelands concerns, and North Brunswick and East Brunswick in Middlesex County enacted bans the same week. Advocacy groups now count roughly 38 New Jersey municipalities that have blocked data centers by local ordinance — the most of any state. On August 27, 2026 Governor Sherrill signed S3379/A4096, requiring data center owners and operators to file semi-annual water and energy usage reports with the BPU for at least three years (extendable), covering total and cooling/IT energy consumption, peak daily water use, water sources and backup power — completing the second element of her four-part data center plan; the administration simultaneously issued new data center guidance for municipalities.

states.name: New Mexico
states.summary: New Mexico Democratic lawmakers have announced a statewide data center moratorium bill for the 2027 session and gave it its first public airing on August 11, 2026 before the interim Science, Technology and Telecommunications Committee. The driver is Project Jupiter in Doña Ana County — the roughly 2.5 GW Oracle and OpenAI campus that is among the largest data center projects in the country. Republicans on the committee pushed back: Sen. Jay Block (R-Rio Rancho) called for a formal economic impact statement on jobs, investment and tax revenue that a moratorium would forgo. states.name: New York
states.summary: New York now has the nation's first statewide data center moratorium, imposed by executive action. On July 14, 2026 Governor Hochul signed Executive Order No. 62, directing DEC to hold in abeyance all new and pending discretionary permits and approvals for data centers of 50 MW or greater that were not deemed complete before the order took effect. The pause runs until the Department of Public Service completes a Generic Environmental Impact Statement (GEIS) on energy demand, water use and air quality and DEC issues a findings statement — framed as up to one year. The EO also directs Empire State Development to publish a Community Investment Framework within 60 days, directs DPS to convene a Data Center Interconnection Working Group within 60 days and to consider a Grid Acceleration Fund, and requires DEC to report on water withdrawal regulations within 12 months. It exempts manufacturing, quantum and biomedical research, accredited universities and Empire AI, and medical facilities. Separately, the legislature's Responsible Data Center Development Act (S10642/A11560) — which passed both chambers on June 4, 2026 and reaches further than the EO, covering 20 MW+ facilities and adding separate utility rate classes and impact studies — had still not been delivered to or acted on by the Governor as of July 20. Hochul has until December 31, 2026 to act once it is delivered; Assembly Speaker Heastie has said he remains hopeful she will sign it, while her office has called the bill 'complicated.' Hochul has also signaled she will seek legislation repealing the state sales tax exemption for large data centers. Local pauses continue to layer on top of the state action: the Brookhaven Town Board voted unanimously on July 16, 2026 for an 18-month moratorium running to January 2028, and East Fishkill froze large projects through 2029 in early July — together putting a roughly $1 billion Long Island data center proposal in limbo. As of late August 2026 the Responsible Data Center Development Act remained unsigned; Governor Hochul has until December 31 to act once it is delivered, and her office has called the bill complicated. Her Executive Order No. 62 moratorium is in force in the meantime, and she has floated adding a decommissioning bond requirement. Genesee County has challenged the pause over its effect on the $19.5 billion Stream U.S. Data Centers project. Local governments continue to mirror the state action: the Town of Tonawanda approved a one-year moratorium in early August 2026 on data centers with peak demand of 20 MW or more. On August 24, 2026, 60 members of the Assembly and Senate, led by Assemblymember Didi Barrett and Senator Kristen Gonzalez, sent Hochul a letter urging her to sign the Responsible Data Center Development Act. Locally, Orangetown's Town Board approved a six-month moratorium on new data center and battery storage applications in late August, exempting DataBank's in-progress expansion.

states.name: Ohio
states.summary: Ohio legislators are reviewing data center energy and community impacts. In April 2026, the Ohio Ballot Board approved a statewide constitutional amendment initiative — the 'Prohibition of Construction of a Data Center' — allowing signature collection to begin. The initiative would ban data centers exceeding 25 MW; as of mid-June 2026 organizers had gathered only roughly 70,000 signatures — far short of the 413,488 valid signatures required by the July 1, 2026 deadline, so the initiative failed to qualify for the 2026 ballot; backers said they plan to resume the effort in 2027. The fight has shifted to municipal ballots: on July 15, 2026 Sunbury City Council unanimously certified a citizen-initiated charter amendment to the November 3, 2026 ballot that would cap data center peak load at 25 MW — effectively blocking a planned $2 billion Amazon campus — and Pataskala residents are pursuing a similar fall vote. Columbus is drafting regulations requiring water conservation plans and developer-funded sewer upgrades. On July 24, 2026 Governor Mike DeWine signed on to the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge, committing to keep data center utility and infrastructure costs off consumers. On August 4, 2026 Rep. Jennifer Gross introduced House Bill 983, the Data Center Accountability and Citizen Protection Act, which would require a local citizen vote before any new data center is built, set environmental standards, regulate cooling water use, and require facilities to supply their own electricity — applying retroactively to more than 150 existing Ohio data centers. In late August 2026 Pataskala's City Council unanimously rejected Aligned Data Centers' 200 MW site plan over unresolved power supply questions; a November ballot measure will ask voters whether large data centers should be permitted in the city. In early September 2026 Miamisburg's council voted 6-0 for a nine-month moratorium and Newton Falls enacted a 12-month moratorium 4-0.

Oklahoma City also enacted a moratorium through end of 2026. Sand Springs faced recall efforts after rezoning for a Google data center. On August 10, 2026 Cherokee Nation Principal Chief Chuck Hoskin Jr. banned hyperscale data centers on tribally owned and trust lands, following a task force report in which 64% of nearly 1,600 tribal citizens surveyed opposed the facilities; projects on non-tribal land within the reservation boundaries now require consultation with the tribal government. Lesly Muñoz (D-Woodburn) and Farrah Chaichi (D-Beaverton), joined by two candidates — announced they will introduce a three-year moratorium on new large data centers in the 2027 legislative session that begins in January. They cited energy and water demand, farmland loss, tax fairness, weak community benefits, and a lack of industry transparency. The Oregon Working Families Party, the Democratic Socialists of America, conservation groups and farm owners are backing the call, and sponsors expect more co-sponsors as the session approaches. The proposal follows the Legislature's March 2026 one-year pause on the state's data center tax incentive program, which had previously saved operators hundreds of millions of dollars. On August 24, 2026 Governor Tina Kotek said she will propose her own data center legislation in the 2027 session, incorporating recommendations from her Data Center Advisory Committee — meaning the session will open with both the legislators' three-year moratorium bill and a governor's bill in play.

states.name: Pennsylvania
states.summary: Pennsylvania moved from disclosure requirements to gatekeeping in August 2026. On August 18, 2026 Governor Josh Shapiro signed Executive Order 2026-05, directing the Department of Environmental Protection to review a data center permit application only if the developer has made a legally binding commitment to the Governor's Responsible Infrastructure Development (GRID) Requirements and has already obtained local government approval. The order also removes AI data center proposals from the state's Fast Track permitting program and prohibits the use of nondisclosure agreements on data center projects. The GRID Requirements cover energy affordability, environmental protection, workforce and economic development, transparency, and community engagement; projects that accept them get expedited review, while non-compliant projects face prolonged permitting. The state has roughly 100 pending proposals and has issued only about five permits. Critics on both sides said the order falls short — of a moratorium on one side, and of predictability for developers on the other. The order builds on the first statutory regulation, enacted July 12, 2026 when Shapiro signed the $50.8B FY2026-27 budget with the substance of SB 146 and HB 1924 folded in: data centers with peak demand of 10 MW or more must file annual electricity and water reports with fines up to $10,000 per day, and the PUC gained authority to review and validate the load forecasts utilities submit to PJM. The stand-alone bills — HB 2150 (passed the House 133-68 in April), HB 2151, HB 1834, HB 2496, HB 1667 and the GRID Standards bill HB 2650 — remain stalled in the Republican-led Senate, and Sen. Katie Muth's three-year hyperscale moratorium bill is still in introduction phase. Locally, Bedford Township adopted a 20-page ordinance in early August covering setbacks, lighting, noise limits, environmental impacts and electricity use, and Pocono Township eliminated its data center overlay district in July. Locally, Doylestown Township unanimously advanced a draft ordinance in late August limiting data centers to conditional uses in light-industrial districts (adoption possible in October), and Salem Township scheduled an August 28 vote on expanding a data center overlay zone for Glenbrook Group's proposed 39-building, $1.4 billion campus. West Hempfield Township (Lancaster County) approved Ordinance 6-26 in early September 2026, limiting data center size and proximity to residential and agricultural areas.

states.name: Texas
states.summary: Texas now has an effective statewide pause on new data center grid connections. On August 3, 2026 Governor Greg Abbott directed the Public Utility Commission of Texas and ERCOT to conduct a comprehensive verification and audit of every data center advancing through ERCOT's interconnection queue, and ERCOT halted its 'batch zero' large-load transmission planning study (which reviews requests of 75 MW or more) until the review concludes. State officials say roughly 250-300 projects representing about 200 GW of requested demand — more than twice ERCOT's all-time peak — are covered, and that the audit will take several months; developers must disclose state financial assistance, power and water use projections, generation sources, ownership, and community impact mitigation. Projects outside ERCOT or relying purely on behind-the-meter generation may fall outside the directive. Local action accelerated in parallel. On June 16, 2026 the San Marcos City Council voted 4-3 to make data centers ineligible in every zoning district — the first outright municipal ban in Texas — a move State Sen. Paul Bettencourt says exceeds the city's authority under Texas preemption law. Fort Worth's City Council voted unanimously on August 11, 2026 to begin a 90-day moratorium and a three-part regulatory plan including an 11-member Data Center and Infrastructure Commission, with findings due November 3 and a final vote set for February 16, 2027. Keller voted unanimously on August 19 to sue neighboring Westlake over a 1.1 million-square-foot facility sited 506 feet from Keller homes and to start its own 90-day moratorium. El Paso County commissioners approved a resolution on August 18 asking the state for a development pause and expanded county authority, and Austin scheduled a council work session for August 25 on siting, water, noise and lighting rules. Hill County's May 2026 county moratorium was rescinded in June after a developer sued for more than $100 million, and Tom Green County abandoned its own effort in response — a reminder that county-level pauses remain legally fragile in Texas. In Lubbock, the city accepted a citizen petition on August 26 for an 18-month moratorium on high-water, high-energy data centers, with a September 8 public hearing and a 30-day window for the council to adopt or reject it. Austin held a council work session August 25 on siting, water, noise and lighting rules.

states.name: Vermont
states.summary: Governor Phil Scott vetoed H.727, the Sustainable Data Center Deployment Act, on May 28, 2026, citing existing Act 250, Public Utility Commission, and municipal zoning authority. The bill had passed with tripartisan support (Senate 26-3, near-unanimous House voice vote) and would have required utility contracts insulating other ratepayers from large-data-center costs, additional site analysis, and climate-fund payments. Lawmakers voted 83-52 to override on May 28 — six votes short of the 90 needed. Vermont's S.205 (100 MW+ AI data center moratorium through July 2030) remained in committee. Governor Scott was also one of only three governors — with Florida's DeSantis and New Hampshire's Ayotte — who declined to sign the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge when it was expanded on July 23, 2026.

states.name: Virginia
states.summary: Virginia's HB 1515 moratorium was carried over to the 2027 session (effectively dead for 2026), and HB 2084 directing the SCC to review data center rate classifications was enacted. The months-long budget standoff over the roughly $1.6 billion data center sales tax exemption ended in late June: the General Assembly passed a ~$205 billion biennial budget on June 22, 2026 (Senate 23-16, House 71-22) that retained the exemption but added a first-of-its-kind energy consumption tax on data centers of $0.011 per kWh consumed monthly, capped at $600 million per year to the general fund. Governor Spanberger proposed budget amendments — including new water-conservation requirements for future data centers — which the legislature approved on June 29, and she signed the budget on June 30, 2026, ending the impasse before the July 1 fiscal deadline. Virginia remains the world's largest data center market. Local activity continued into late July: on July 21, 2026 Loudoun County asked the State Corporation Commission to stay its approval of a Dominion Energy transmission line while settlement talks with Dominion and the school system proceed, and on July 22 the Pittsylvania County Board approved a resolution supporting STACK Infrastructure's $100 billion Berry Hill megasite campus — roughly 2,990 acres to be built out over 15 to 30 years. In a July 31, 2026 order made public in early August, the State Corporation Commission ruled that large-load data centers must pay for transmission facilities built solely to serve them — costs previously spread across all customers through the Rider T-1 line item — resolving a dispute over roughly $1.5 billion in Dominion Energy transmission spending and cutting the average residential monthly increase from about $2.90 to $0.94. Dominion has 90 days to file a new cost-assignment proposal. Local restriction also hardened: Chesapeake's City Council unanimously approved a zoning ordinance on August 19, 2026 limiting data centers to conditional uses in industrial zones, banning groundwater use, closing by-right development loopholes and removing the Fentress Overlay exception, with an eight-month application pause still in effect and nearly 40 residents testifying. Loudoun County supervisors voted 6-1 in July to draft a temporary moratorium, with a vote set for September 15, while Amazon filed a by-right site plan for four buildings on the former GWU campus to bypass planning commission review. In Franklin County, the Project Flash campus was cancelled in mid-August after developer negotiations failed amid opposition from more than 40 speakers. Henry County adopted a strict Data Center District ordinance on August 25, 2026, requiring rezoning plus a special use permit, 1,000-foot setbacks from non-industrial properties, a 50 dBA noise limit, closed-loop cooling only, and mandatory water-use studies.

states.name: Washington
states.summary: Washington enacted SB 5982 requiring large data center customers to meet the same clean energy deadlines as utilities and directing the UTC to establish reporting requirements. HB 2515 — a broader data center regulation bill — passed the House 51-41 but died in the Senate after Microsoft and other tech companies opposed it. Local activity has accelerated dramatically: Seattle Councilmembers Juarez, Lin, and Council President Hollingsworth introduced a 365-day emergency moratorium on new large (10 MW+) data centers; the Council passed the emergency ~1-year moratorium 9-0 on June 9, 2026, and Spokane followed with its own one-year citywide moratorium (6-1) on June 23. Two developers had withdrawn Seattle expansion plans amid the backlash, and Mayor Wilson announced parallel administrative steps on May 1. In late July 2026 Spokane County proposed extending the pause to unincorporated areas with a nine-month building permit moratorium expiring after the 2027 legislative session. Spokane County commissioners unanimously approved a four-month moratorium on new data center permits on August 19, 2026 — trimmed from an earlier nine-month proposal — to let staff draft zoning regulations, with the option to extend depending on the outcome of commission elections. Yakima County commissioners unanimously directed staff on August 4 to draft a six-month moratorium after residents raised water scarcity concerns, despite no applications pending. Port Angeles' council voted 5-1 in early September 2026 to direct staff to draft a six-month moratorium on new data center applications.

states.name: Wisconsin
states.summary: The Wisconsin 2025-26 legislature ended its session without passing a statewide data center bill: a GOP ratepayer/water-protection measure (AB 840) passed the Assembly 53-44 but died in the Senate, and a Democratic 'very large customer' rate-class bill did not advance. Local action continues to accelerate — Dodge County adopted an 18-month moratorium in early June 2026 (29-2), and the Sheboygan Common Council passed a moratorium on zoning and building permits for data centers over 10,000 square feet on July 23, 2026 — joining Port Washington's first-in-the-nation anti-data-center referendum ban and moratoria in Madison, Manitowoc County, and Driftless Area townships. Local pauses kept spreading in August 2026. La Crosse's Plan Commission advanced an 18-month moratorium on August 3, with a public hearing August 5 and a Common Council vote August 13, and Bellevue's village board voted unanimously on August 10 for a one-year moratorium extendable by six months — joining nearby Wrightstown and Manitowoc County. Opposition also grew to two natural gas plants proposed to power data centers in Kenosha and Walworth counties, after a UW-Madison study estimated $1.38 billion in nationwide health harms over their 30-year lifetimes.

states.name: Wyoming
states.summary: Wyoming has taken no statewide legislative action to restrict data centers and remains generally favorable to large-load development, but local governments have begun to engage. Cheyenne rejected a proposed moratorium in May 2026. In late July 2026, Park County commissioners proposed requiring special-use permits for data centers and other heavy electrical-load users as part of the county's first land-use overhaul in more than a decade, despite no project having been proposed there. The state also hosts the planned 1,250 MW Prometheus Hyperscale campus. Cheyenne's City Council annexed and zoned a 34.46-acre parcel on August 10, 2026 as a staging area for North Range Business Park data center construction, over resident objections about aquifers, noise and incremental annexation; a citizen petition drive on data center limits neared its signature threshold in early August. On September 1, 2026 Laramie County commissioners approved a Planned Unit Development zone change for Vantage Data Centers' 'Project Latigo,' a $20 billion, 1,835-acre campus south of Cheyenne with on-site natural gas generation and closed-loop cooling, projected to create up to 2,000 jobs.
